accuracy.evidence: Restricted rotation is explained by the π bond formed from sideways p-orbital overlap; the quoted barrier of about 270 kJ/mol matches the C=C minus C–C mean bond enthalpy gap (614 − 347 kJ/mol) and the measured ethene torsion barrier. CIP ranking uses atomic number of the attached atom, then the set of next atoms at the first point of difference (CH₂CH₃ (C,H,H) over CH₃ (H,H,H); CH₂OH (O,H,H) over CH₂CH₃). Boiling points of Z- and E-but-2-ene (3.7 and 0.9 °C) are rounded to 4 and 1 °C. Every challenge molecule's E/Z label was worked by hand and agrees with the lab's verdict function.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips from AQA/OCR examiner reports: ranking by group size or mass (CH₃ thought to beat Cl or Br), assuming cis always equals Z (2-bromobut-2-ene step and challenge trap), treating a methyl/ethyl tie as no priority, checking only one carbon for two different groups (but-1-ene, 2-methylbut-2-ene), and believing a C=C can rotate like C–C.

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanics are specific to stereochemistry about C=C: a twist drag that springs back with fading p-orbital overlap while a C–C flips, swapping groups on one carbon to interconvert E and Z, tap-to-rank CIP priority with atomic-number and next-atom explanations, and a palette builder with a live E/Z verdict. Nothing is shared with the structural isomer peg board (flagiso) or the alkene addition lab, and the distinctness gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: Learners discover the rules by acting: the C=C refuses to turn while the C–C turns, so the lock is seen before it is named; swapping on but-1-ene returns the same molecule, revealing the two-different-groups test; wrong priority taps explain the atomic-number rule using the actual atoms; making Z from 2-bromobut-2-ene shows CH₃ groups ending up opposite. Each step closes with a one-sentence rule.

predictions.evidence: Six locked predictions with tempting wrong options: a C=C turns freely, one but-2-ene, but-1-ene gives an E form, CH₃ beats Br because it is bigger, CH₃ vs C₂H₅ is a tie, and same-side CH₃ groups mean Z. In each case the lab then shows the opposite and the reveal refers to the learner's pick.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Ten rotating molecules; wrong answers get one of five specific messages: identical groups on one carbon (no E/Z), two different groups on each carbon (there are isomers), go to the next atoms on a tie, comparing matching groups is cis/trans thinking, and rank by atomic number not size. Each message quotes the real atoms, e.g. 'Br beats CH₃: Br has atomic number 35, C has 6.'

readability.evidence: Kid text scores Flesch-Kincaid grade 3.5 and adult text 6.9 on the repo's readability tool, inside the learner limits of 6.5 and 9.5. Technical words (π bond, p orbital, zusammen, entgegen) are each glossed in the sentence where they first appear.

no_filler.evidence: The content gate found no filler phrases. Kid paragraphs cover why C=C is locked, the but-2-ene pair with boiling points, the two-different-groups test, and priority plus E/Z naming; adult paragraphs give the definition, what the lab does, the named mistakes and typical exam asks.

mobile.evidence: Checked on 360 px Android screenshots in light and dark themes and on desktop: group pills are 32 px tall with 34 px tap radius, the build palette wraps to two rows below the molecule, the verdict text was moved clear of the top groups after the first screenshot showed an overlap, and every canvas action has a full-width button twin.

accessibility.evidence: axe reported no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in either theme in the walkthrough. The canvas aria-label states every group's slot, bond type and the live E/Z verdict; twist, swap, priority picks, slot choice and every palette group have labelled buttons, and challenge feedback is in a polite live region.

sources: AQA A-level Chemistry specification 7405, section 3.3.1.3 Isomerism
